properties.Name: The Auditorium Building
properties.Address: 161 Mill St, Grass Valley
properties.Desc_:
Plaque dedicated 2017 by Native Sons of the Golden West: The Auditorium Building. On July 30, 1896, a fire started here at the site of Argall's Opera House, owned by Charles E. Clinch, burning the entire block on East Mill Street from Neal to Bank. In 1900, an incorporation composed of the Native Sons of the Golden West, Ancient Order of the Foresters, Knights of Pythias, Red Men, and the Miner's Union was formed to build a fine theater of three stories. The first floor held a magnificent theater with a capacity of 600 on the floor and 250 in the gallery and office space for the Grass Valley City Hall. The second story was devoted to lodge rooms and the third story was a banquet hall. The basement housed both the kitchen and the armory for Company 1 of the National Guard. On February 2, 1901, the Auditorium Theater opened to a week-long celebration and operated until November 12, 1922. Two days later, it reopened as the Strand Movie Theater, operating until April 22, 1942. The building was then home of the F. S. Rasco & Co. store and since 1972 has been home to Hedman/Ashley furniture store.

properties.Name: Idaho-Maryland Mine Site
properties.Address: Hillside adjacent to Centennial Dr and Whispering Pines Lane, south of Idaho Maryland Rd, Grass Valley
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1984 by Nevada County, NEV 33. Description: The Idaho quartz mine was discovered in 1863. It prospered under the Coleman brothers from 1867-93, then consolidated with the Maryland and other small mines. Eventually it became one of the 'Big Three' of the Northern Mines, the other two being the Empire and the North Star. Its final years under the management of Errol MacBoyle were very productive. He developed a revolutionary method of shaft sinking, using a huge core drill called the Newsom drilling machine. World War II and government order L208 brought about final closing.

Note: Various parts of the mine still exist. The office building is off the east side of Centennial Drive, between Idaho Maryland Road and Whispering Pines Lane. A headframe is located near the Grass Valley Scrap, Iron & Metal yard.

Learn more about the mine from Gold in Quartz: The Legendary Idaho Maryland Mine by Jack Clark, or from MacBoyle's Gold by Gage McKinney, both available from Comstock Bonanza Press.

Beryl's continuing career in public service has already spanned the terms of seven presidents, six governors and three-dozen council members. A Mason, Rotarian and Elk, Beryl has brought a sense of commitment and purpose to his life matched by few and bettered by none.

properties.Name: Ten Stamp Mill
properties.Address: City parking lot on Commercial St, west of York St, Nevada City
properties.Desc_:
Plaque dedicated 2006 by Native Sons of the Golden West: "Six tall, upright rods of iron, as large as a man's ankle, and heavily shod with a mass of iron and steel at their lower ends . . .". So begins Mark Twain's description of a Nevada stamp mill. ". . . These rose and fell, one after the other, in a ponderous dance, in an iron box called a battery." Each of the stamps weighed 600 pounds. "One of us stood by the battery all day long, breaking up masses of silver-bearing rock with a sledge and shoveling it in."
At the end of his brief stint shoveling ore into the Nevada stamp mill, Twain told his boss he thought the $10 a week was not quite enough. He asked for a new wage of $400,000 a month. He didn't get it and had to become a newspaperman.

This ten stamp mill stands just two blocks from where it was manufactured at Miners Foundry in 1904. It operated at the Alpha mine in Sierra County from 1905 until 1931. Each stamp weighs 1,000 pounds and was used to crush gold-bearing rock. Gary Cope recovered the stamp mill in 1975. It was bought and erected on this site, Native Sons Park, by Hydraulic Parlor No. 56 of the Native Sons of the Golden West with the help of the Historic Preservation Foundation of the N.S.G.W. in 2005.

properties.Name: Searls Law Office
properties.Address: 214 Church St,  Nevada City
properties.Desc_:
Text of plaque Landmark registered 1972 by Nevada County, NEV 15. Plaque dedicated 1972 by Native Sons of the Golden West: This building completed December 18, 1872, was the law office for three generations of this family. Niles Searls, who arrived in 1851, practiced law here from 1872 to 1885. He had been elected district attorney in 1855, then district judge for Nevada, Sierra and Yuba counties, then became Chief Justice of the California Supreme Court in 1887. Fred Searls, his son, held the longest tenure in this building (1879-1929). He drafted the first incorporation papers of the hydroelectric industry of California. Carroll Searls, son of Fred, practiced here from 1915 to 1923; later became general counsel of the Newmont Mining Company in New York City; used this office until November 4,1970.

Note: Niles Searls was elected district attorney in 1852, not 1855, but because he left California and went east to marry before his term of office began, William M. Stewart was appointed to fill the vacancy. Later, when Stewart resigned in 1854 to become the acting state attorney general, Searls was appointed to replace him as district attorney. From 1972 until 2014 the building housed the Historical Society's Searls Historical Library and Archives.

properties.Name: Railroad and Transportation Museum
properties.Address: Five Kidder Court, Nevada City. Take Ridge Rd exit off Hwy 49
properties.Desc_:
First plaque placed 2001 by Nevada City Council: Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad Museum and Interpretive Center. The Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad (1876–1942) ran 22 miles from Nevada City through Grass Valley, its headquarters; to Colfax, Placer County, where it met the transcontinental line of the Central (later Southern) Pacific Railroad. Built by John F. Kidder, it was the main freight and passenger route serving the western county. Kidder ran the railroad until his death in 1901 and was followed by his widow Sarah, who became the first woman railroad president in United States. She served until 1913. This museum is dedicated to preserving the NCNGRR's place in history and to those who built, operated and maintained the little road.

Second plaque dedicated 2011 by Native Sons of the Golden West: Railroad and Transportation Museum. The Nevada County Historical Society founded the Transportation Museum Division in 1983 to acquire, document, restore and preserve information and artifacts pertaining to Nevada County's railroad and transportation history. Best known is the Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad that operated from 1876 until 1942. The museum opened for public enjoyment on March 17, 2003.

properties.Name: Glasson House
properties.Address: 515 W. Main St. Grass Valley
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 2005 by Nevada County, NEV 05-01. Description: This Victorian/Greek Revival house was built in 1866 for Miles P. O'Connor, who came to California in 1849 and to Nevada County in 1852. He served as justice of the peace for Little York township in 1852-53 and for Grass Valley 1862-69. He served one term in the state assembly and two in the state senate. He earned a fortune from the famous Idaho gold mine and was instrumental in creation of the Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad. After selling this house to John Polglase in 1873, he moved to San Jose and funded various institutions, including a sanitarium later known as O'Connor Hospital. John Polglase, a hard-rock miner from Cornwall, came to Grass Valley in 1864. In 1875 Polglase bought an interest in John Glasson's grocery and provisions store while continuing to work underground in the Idaho mine. In 1882 he sold the house to his partner, and Glasson and his heirs owned it from then until 1973. John Glasson, like Polglase, came here in 1864 from England, and like O'Connor he played a prominent role in Nevada County history. He bought the local gas company in 1885-86 and in 1888 merged it with the Grass Valley Electric Light and Motor Co. He built the county's first hydroelectric plant at Deer Creek Falls and was a director and treasurer of the Narrow Gauge railroad. His daughter Bernice was a major benefactor to the Sierra Nevada Memorial Hospital, and she lived in this house until her death in 1966.

Located: 515 W. Main St, Grass Valley CA

properties.Name: Saint Paul Lutheran Church Site
properties.Address: St. Paul Pl. east of Hwy 174 at Chicago Park. St. Paul Cemetery is first left past the fire station
properties.Desc_:
Plaque dedicated 1993 by Grace Lutheran Church, Missouri Synod: On this site donated by Anna Pusheck the German Evangelical Lutheran St. Paul congregation was established in 1902 for worship and praise to God, continuing until 1984.

Landmark registered 2020 by Nevada County, NEV 20-06. Second plaque dedicated 2022 by Grace Lutheran Church. "On this site in 1902, the German Evangelical Lutheran St. Paul Church and Cemetery were established on land donated by Anna Pusheck and her son Charles, two of the founders of Chicago Park. The church served a German-American population residing in Auburn, Weimar, Reno and Chicago Park. Services for the primarily German-American Lutheran congregation were conducted in German prior to 1924. Following that, both German and English were used in all church activities until World War II, when anti-German sentiment prompted the use of English only. In 1971, children playing with matches set fire to the church and it was destroyed. The parsonage was converted to a church and services were held there until 1984, at which time the congregation joined with their sister church, Grace Lutheran in Grass Valley. Interment in the St. Paul Cemetery remains available to members of Grace Lutheran Church."

Note: In 1895, Dr. Charles Pusheck built a sanitarium in Chicago Park, which he later converted to a hotel. The St. Paul Lutheran church building was dedicated in December 1904. Most services and record keeping were in the German language until 1924. From then until 1942 both English and German were used to compile important data, and English services were held once a month. An English-language hymnal was used for the first time on September 28, 1924.

properties.Address: 102 W Main St Grass Valley

Plaque dedicated 1986 by Marie I Johnson: Operated by pioneer druggist William Loutzenheiser (1824–1905) and son, John G. (1861-1929). The pharmacy began here in a wooden building in 1851. The structure gave way to the present brick edifice in the fall of 1855. William was a member of the 1861 city Board of Trustees, one of the original locators of the Idaho Quartz claim, and was active in several other mining ventures. On July 4, 1887 the pharmacy was the site of a bloody duel between two Grass Valley merchants, Henry Sylvester and John Davis, in which the latter was killed. In 1928 the business changed hands after 77 years of continuous operation by the Loutzenheiser family. Between 1928 and 1966 the building had many tenants. In the fall of 1966 Marie Johnson, known as the Flower Lady, founded Foothill Flowers. The interior of the building was destroyed by fire in May 1984 and was subsequently remodeled.

The University of California was born at the church in 1853, when Henry Durant took part in a convention of Congregationalists and Presbyterians who resolved to establish a college in California. properties.Desc_:
Plaque dedicated 2002 by Masons: Masonry in Grass Valley. Madison Lodge #23  was established under dispensation from the Grand Lodge of California on May 4th 1852. Its permanent charter was issued on May 5th 1853. Madison Lodge held its first two meetings at the old Columbus School on the present site of Hennessy School. The Lodge moved to a building on the south side of Main St.  where it now meets Auburn St.  This wooden building was destroyed along with most of Grass Valley in the great fire of September 12 and 13, 1855. A few days later, the Masons met with the Odd Fellows to select a site for a new brick building to house both organizations at 110 Mill St. This building was Madison's home for nearly 73 years, until fire destroyed the Masonic portion of the building in December 1928. For the next nine years the Lodge met in the auditorium of the old Strand Theater at 161 Mill St.  During this time, planning was being completed for our present building, which saw its first meeting on January 29, 1938. For 150 years, in both good times and bad, through 7 wars and a great depression, the Masonic spirit of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth has continued on through our brethren of honorable men of all backgrounds, professions and faith. This plaque was set on 9 May 2002 in rededication ceremonies conducted by C. Ray Whitaker, Grand Master of Masons in California and Elmer B. Curtis, Master of Madison Lodge.

properties.Address: 330 Alexander St, Nevada City
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered Oct. 13, 2020 by Nevada County, NEV 20-04. Plaque dedicated 2021 by The NC Historical Society. "THE PRESTON AND LOUISA ALEXANDER HOMESITE. Preston Alexander, one of Nevada City's earliest African American settlers, purchased this property along Buckeye Ravine on May 19, 1859.  The property was occupied by Preston (1834-1889), his wife, Louisa (1838-1902), and their five children, John, Mary Amelia, Horatio Henry, Louisa, and Rosella Elizabeth, until 1902.  The Alexander family was well respected and highly regarded in the community.  They were members of the African Methodist Episcopal (A.M.E.) Churches in Nevada City and Grass Valley.  Preston Alexander was active in the major civil rights movements of the mid-19th century: abolishing slavery nationally, winning the franchise for African American men, gaining the right for African Americans to testify in court, and securing their access to public accommodations.  Alexander Street is named in their honor."

Text of plaque: Native Daughters Garden in George Calanan Park. In 1922, Laurel Parlor No. 6, Native Daughters of the Golden West acquired two small lots to create a memorial park for the veterans and those who died in World War I. In the interest of 'a valuable public improvement,' Laurel Parlor sold the lot to the U.S. Forest Service for a district office in 1936. The advent of World War II redirected federal resources and the planned 6,000 square foot building was never constructed. The lot remained a community park. In 1967, the park was dedicated to honor George Humphrey Calanan (1872- 1951), a much-loved Town Trustee (City Councilman), health officer, assessor, volunteer fireman, and long time City Clerk. He was known as 'the man who got things done.' The park was granted to the City of Nevada City by the United States Department of the Interior on December 1, 1971.

properties.Address: 319 Neal St, corner of S. Church St, Grass Valley
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1975 by Nevada County, NEV 28. Plaque dedicated 1995 by Native Daughters and Native Sons of the Golden West: Homesite of Caroline Mead Hanson. Whose idea sparked the annual Donation Day sponsored by Grass Valley Ladies Relief Society since 1883.

Note: Home of the originator of Grass Valley's Donation Day, that began In 1883. Mrs. Hansen, an invalid, sat in the bay window of her home and watched the children troop to school. Hearing of the Ladies Relief Society's shortage of funds she suggested a plan to help the needy share the Feast of Christmas. Each child would bring a stick of wood and a potato to school on the same day named by the school superintendent. The potatoes would be put in a sack provided by the janitor; the wood would be piled in the school yard. On the following day these donations would be removed by the Relief Society and dispensed as needed. Mrs. Hansen conveyed her plan in a letter to the Grass Valley Daily Union that was published November 20, 1883. Since that date thousands of Grass Valley school children and citizens have marched in the Donation Day parade.

properties.Address: 401 Broad St, Nevada City
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered by State of California in 1972, CHL 863. Designated a National Historic Landmark 1973. First plaque dedicated 1968 by Chap 10 E Clampus Vitus: Opened Sept. 11, 1865 with comic Dan Setchell and dancers Worrell Sisters. Built by Geo. S. Pierce. Mark Twain, Emma Nevada, Jack London, Gilbert Barry and Richard Jose performed here. Movies shown from 1908-1958 Acquired 1967 by Liberal Arts Commission for restoration.

Second plaque dedicated 1974 by State of California in cooperation with the Nevada County Historical Landmarks and Liberal Arts Commissions: "California's oldest existing theatre building, the Nevada, opened September 9, 1865. Celebrities such as Mark Twain, Jack London and Emma Nevada have appeared on its stage. Closed in 1957, the theatre was later purchased through public donations and reopened May 17, 1968 to again serve the cultural needs of the community."

Third plaque dedicated 2022 by the Landmarks Commission: "This plaque is dedicated to Sara 'Sally' Lewis (1914) the preservation pioneer of Nevada City and Nevada County. Sally and Dr. Leland Lewis retired to Nevada City in 1963 from Bakersfield. Sally was a charter member of the Nevada City Liberal Arts Commission formed to save the Nevada Theatre from demolition. The Theatre's 100th anniversary in 1965 was celebrated with a locally produced play 'Golden Days', a gala Dinner and Ball to establish the building fund which led to the preservation of the Nevada Theatre. Sally was a founding member and the First Chair of the Nevada County Historical Landmarks Commission created by the Board of Supervisors in April 1969. She served as Chair until 1983, during which time over 30 landmarks were registered on the County, State, Federal preservation lists. Sally was honored at the Landmarks Commission's 50th anniversary celebration in April, 2019. Ed Tyson, curator of the Searls Library, said of Sally, 'If we took the people involved in Nevada City, Nevada County and rated them 1 through 10 for their effectiveness, I would rate her as a 10.'
Sally passed away in March of 2000 and is buried in the North Columbia Cemetery beside husband Leland and son Chris."

Note: Jack London's appearance in the Nevada Theatre is undocumented and Gilbert Barry's may be a Clamper fabrication. The is no North Columbia Cemetery; the Lewis family is buried in the North Bloomfield Cemetery.

properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1939 by State of California, CHL 298. Designated a National Historical Landmark 1977. Plaque dedicated 1963 by Native Daughters of the Golden West: This plaque marks the site of the Empire Mine, noted for its continuous operation 1850-1957 producing over $120,000,000 in gold.

Note: The Empire Mine was originally located by George D. Roberts in October 1850. In the spring of 1854 the Empire Mining Company was incorporated and in 1865 new works were erected, including a 30-stamp mill. In 1869 Wm. B. Bourn Sr. purchased the Empire. When he died Wm. B. Bourn Jr. took over the management of the mine. In 1929 the Empire mine and the adjacent North Star mine were consolidated and became known as the Empire Star mine. The Empire Mine was the oldest quartz mine in continuous operation in the United States, having been in constant operation since 1850 to the late 1950s, but like all U.S. gold mines, it was shut down during World War II, except for a maintenance crew and some limited operation. On July 1,1945, the mine was again allowed to go into full production. An auction was held on September 25 and 26,1959, to sell the buildings and contents. The State of California purchased the Empire mine properties in 1975 for use as a state park.

properties.Desc_:
Text of plaque: "It was at this location on the afternoon of June 5, 1880 that a fire erupted in John White's upholstery shop. More than fifty buildings - including the nearby New York Hotel and most of the Chinese Quarter - were destroyed within an hour, but from the ashes of that conflagration a new business district emerged and York Street was created to ensure better downtown fire protection. Then, early in the 20th century, a doctor's office was established here. The longest-serving physician to occupy this corner was Bernard W. Hummelt, MD (1906 - 1998), who, between 1934 and his retirement in 1988, practiced internal medicine, orthopedics and general surgery. Over the course of his lengthy career he delivered over 1500 Nevada County babies. Dr. Hummelt was among the earliest physicians in the nation to administer penicillin and was instrumental in the founding of Sierra Nevada Memorial Hospital - where he served as its third Chief of Staff." The church's founders were Dennis Drummond Carter, Samuel Rodgers, Elijah Booth, John Hamilton, and James Jenkins. The original building was destroyed in a storm in 1865, but was soon rebuilt by the community. In addition to holding religious services, the church was a center for social, cultural, political and civil rights events, such as the "festivals of freedom" that commemorated the anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation. The building also housed a "Sabbath School" established in 1867. The church was used until 1894, by which time the membership had dwindled and the property was sold and became a series of private residences. properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1996 by Nevada County, NEV 96-03. Description: Nathaniel P. Brown, founding owner of the Nevada Daily Transcript and early political figure in Nevada City, lived here from 1865 until 1909. He expanded the original cottage to its current size in the 1880s, allowing for frequent entertaining. The home was built in 1858 by Jesse S. Wall, an early settler and merchant. Nathaniel Brown came to Nevada City from Massachusetts in 1853 at the age of 18, following his friend Aaron Sargent. He was part owner of the weekly Nevada Journal from 1855 to 1859. In 1860, Brown founded the county's first daily, the Morning Transcript, and from then until 1904 was prominent in newspaper circles and a constant champion of mine owner's rights. The most famous resident of the house was opera diva Emma Nevada. While her father, Dr. W. W. Wixom, sought a new home for his family, Emma and her mother boarded here until 1864. Between the ages of 4 and 13 she resided at Austin, Nevada. Emma Wixom achieved great fame as a singer and took the stage name Nevada to honor the state in which she grew up and the county where she was born. She returned to Nevada City in 1902 and performed to a packed audience at the Nevada Theatre.

Plaque dedicated 2019 by Native Sons of the Golden West: "The Eureka-Idaho-Maryland vein was discovered as a quartz outcropping in 1851. It was worked  successfully by William Watt as the Eureka Mine and later by John and Edward Coleman as the Idaho Mine. In 1893 Samuel P. Dorsey consolidated earlier operations into the Idaho Maryland Mine. After acquiring the mine in 1926, Errol MacBoyle expanded the Idaho Maryland by incorporating the Union Hill Mine and other surrounding claims. Later he incorporated the nearby Brunswick Mine into his operations as well and adopted sophisticated refining equipment. MacBoyle achieved spectacular success and employed more than 1,000 men during the Great Depression of the 1930s. By making the Idaho Maryland one of America's richest gold producers, he set an example for others and the region boomed. Using equipment designed by John B. Newsom, the mine developed a revolutionary method of shaft sinking and in 1936 completed the 1,125-foot Round Hole shaft. Due to rising costs and expanding regulations the Idaho Maryland mine was unable to keep up with their depleting funds and were eventually ordered to close by the State of California in December of 1956."

Note: In the second half of the 19th century, Nevada City had a well-established Chinese Quarter along Commercial St. from Pine St. to the top of Broad St. The Quarter included numerous businesses, such as grocers, doctors and barbers, as well as a temple, brothels, gambling halls and opium houses. Plaque placed 2006 by the Connor family: The Weiss-Hieronimus Brewery Cellar. Beginning in the early 1860s and continuing until Prohibition, the lower portion of this building was the storeroom for keg beer produced first by Emille (sic) Weiss for the Weiss Brewery then by Simon Hieronimus for the Hieronimus Brewery–later known as the Nevada Brewery. As the brewery business grew, Mr. Hieronimus established a bottling plant and stable on property across the street from this building. But keg beer continued to be stored here. A fire in the summer of 1896 destroyed the original house and severely damaged the cellar. But the Nevada Brewery emerged bigger and better than ever. It was at that time that the cellar was enlarged to its present size, a ventilation system installed and refrigeration added. In 2004 the property was acquired by Jesse and Kay Connor, who carefully restored the old brewery cellar and home. This plaque has been placed to honor the legacy of both the Weiss and Hieronimus families and to remind people that the best lager beer in Nevada County was once produced here.

properties.Address: 325 Spring St, Nevada City
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1974 by Nevada County, NEV 21, and 1994 by State of California, CHL 1012.
First plaque dedicated 1966 by Chap 10 E Clampus Vitus: Miners' Foundry (Allan's Machine Shop) Founded 1856. This original brick building in continuous usage as a Foundry for over 100 years. Famous Pelton waterwheel developed and manufactured here in 1878. Ingenious double-cupped bucket design by Lester A. Pelton of Camptonville and Nevada City. It became the basis for hydro-electric turbine generators throughout the world.

Second plaque dedicated 1994 by State of California: Pelton Wheel Manufacturing Site. The Pelton Water Wheel, first commercially manufactured at George Allan's Foundry & Machine Works in 1879 was a major advancement in water power and revolutionized hard rock mining technology. Its unique feature was a series of paired buckets, shaped like bowls or spoons and separated by a splitter, that divided the incoming water into two parts. By the late 1800s, the Pelton Wheels were providing energy to operate water powered machinery throughout the world. In 1888, Lester Pelton moved his business to San Francisco, but granted continuing manufacturing rights to Allan's Foundry, where the wheels were manufactured into the early 1900s, when most local mines shifted to electric power.

Note: Opened in 1855, the foundry was moved to its present location after the fire of 1856, and supplied equipment to the milling shops of many mines. Notable equipment included the Patent Mill Guide installed at the Tonopah Mine in Nevada and a gadget known as the Miners Foundry Ejector that had universal demand. Edward Matteson's hydraulic derrick, used to extract rocks from streams and rivers, was perfected here. Much of our modern electricity comes from generators driven by descendants of the Pelton Wheel. Occupied in the 1970s and 1980s by the American Victorian Museum, the building now houses the Miners Foundry Cultural Center.

Landmark registered 2016 by Nevada County, NEV 16-01. Description: This house was constructed in 1874 by John Boardman, a local pioneer, miner and newspaperman. Born in London, England, in 1828, he emigrated to New Orleans in 1842. In 1849, he left Memphis, Tennessee, where he had been working as a printer, and arrived in Nevada County in March 1850. He initially engaged in mining, then worked at various local newspapers. For a few years, he was the Grass Valley postmaster. In 1858, he married Cecilia Purdy. They had 7 children. He died in 1888.

The property was originally purchased by Richard White in 1869 for a $1000 bag of gold. After several fires, the present building was rebuilt in 1890 by the Ford family, who had purchased the property. It was occupied for much of the 20th century by Miss Savory Ford. The house was then renovated and acquired by the Nienabers. Much of the interior is remarkably authentic for the period. properties.Address: Railroad Avenue at Sacramento St, Nevada City
properties.Desc_:
First plaque to the right of the Kiosk dedicated 1968 by Chap 10 E Clampus Vitus; rededicated 2020 by Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad Museum: "Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad was dedicated May 20, 1876 one hundred feet east of this spot. Built by John Flint Kidder between 1874-76 it ran 22 miles from Nevada City to Colfax via Grass Valley. Rails taken up in 1942. Sarah Kidder, widow of builder, world's first woman railroad president 1901-13."Landmark registered by Nevada County and second plaque on rock to the left of the Kiosk dedicated 2022 by Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad Museum, NEV 22-01: "In the race to build the western portion of the Transcontinental Railroad, the Central Pacific Railroad recruited over ten thousand young men from China, creating a skilled and dependable work force.  Upon completion many of these workers, who had come to America under contract for employment, returned home to China. Others remained to find employment building railroads throughout the United States. This site marks one end of the 22-mile Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad that connected Nevada City and Grass Valley with Colfax and the Central Pacific Railroad. After construction of the NCNGRR started in 1875, over three hundred Chinese immigrants labored to build the railroad. They built the railroad grade over the rugged and uneven terrain between Colfax and Grass Valley, scaling canyons, filling ravines, and prepared the way for bridges and trestles. Using hand tools, horse drawn scrapers, hand carts and their determination, they completed the task in early 1876. Although considered more dependable than white workers, they were paid less. When the railroad was completed in 1876 most of the Chinese moved on to other railroad construction projects; a few Chinese workers remained as track workers maintaining the NCNGRR. Apart from laboring on the railroad, several Chinese businessmen in Nevada City were investors and retained stock in the company into the 20th century. The contributions of Chinese immigrants were an essential element in the building and success of the NCNGRR."

Note: On this site at one end of the Narrow Gauge line stood the Nevada City station. In 2020, the Railroad Museum erected a kiosk which contains several informational panels detailing the history and operation of the Narrow Gauge. It also contains a plaque honoring Madelyn Helling, one of the Museum's founders and longtime directors. The site is sometimes known as Clampers Square.

Built in July of 1850, it was Grass Valley's first business enterprise. Mill and Walsh Streets got their names from this business and this early pioneer. Judge Walsh was elected Justice of the Peace for Grass Valley. He served as Chairman of the Board of Supervisors and State Senator. In later years, Thomas Hodge built the City Brewery on this site which continued to operate under various owners from 1873 to 1909. Hodge was a resident of Grass Valley for 55 years and passed away at his stone Cornish-style cottage located next door, which still exists today. The City Brewery was a thriving business during the Gold Rush, making regular deliveries by wagon to every mining camp within a 30 mile radius."

He mined for a time on Wolf Creek, then worked in a bakery. He became a renter of the business, but after two years sold the bakery operation to Herrman Maurer and bought a half-interest in a brewery with John Frank, operating in the rear of the Western Hotel which burned in 1856. The brick brewery was constructed in 1861, replacing a smaller 1856 frame building on North Auburn Street. Frank Richard bought out the partner in 1861 and was in turn bought out by Binkelmann shortly later. He ran the brewery until his death on May 23, 1894, leaving his wife Sophie to carry on until her death in 1915, when the brewery was bequeathed to her son, David J. Binkelmann.

properties.Name: Memorial Park GV
properties.Address: Memorial Park, corner of Race St and Colfax Ave, Grass Valley
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 2024 by Nevada County, NEV 24-02. "MEMORIAL PARK: GRASS VALLEY'S GREATEST ASSET. At noon on November 11, 1921, bells tolled throughout the City of Grass Valley as over two thousand residents and visitors gathered to attend the opening of Memorial Park. Presided over by Jim Tyrrell, Secretary of the Chamber of Commerce, the ceremony celebrated an unprecedented act of community philanthropy and collaboration that transformed an abandoned pear orchard into a park that would come to be known as the city's greatest asset. The park honored the community's some 450 World War I service members and memorialized its war dead, provided residents with opportunities for recreation and community gatherings and created a destination for automobile tourism. Completed in just under a year, the park was built through the financial generosity, time, and talents of countless volunteers from all walks of life and social positions. No city funds or taxes were used. Visitors arriving at the park found a lushly planted memorial grove to honor the war dead, picnic grounds, a spacious pool with changing rooms, tennis courts, a children's playground, and a travel campground with cottages. Inspired by the park's centennial in 2021, the City of Grass Valley's Historical Commission initiated the creation of the Centennial Courtyard, centrally located around the Saurin King Clocktower, to tell the story of the community's collective act of remembrance and renewal that built Memorial Park. Still enjoyed today by residents and visitors alike, the ever-evolving park keeps alive the motto of the 1921 building campaign, 'In Memory of the Past, We Build for the Future'."

Note: As of the date of this publication, this plaque has not been dedicated. The land and swimming pool were donated by the Empire Mine Co., the club house was donated by the Idaho Maryland Mine Co., and people of the area subscribed $8,000. Frances Jones, a philanthropist and community organizer of humanitarian relief during World War I, helped design and implement the landscaping of Memorial Park. The park contains several other plaques and monuments honoring those who served our country in the armed forces in various wars.

He worked as a carpenter, left to mine at Iowa Hill and finally returned to enter the lumber business. With his brother Dan he set up a saw mill on Little Deer Creek (now Pioneer Park). The enterprise boomed and in 1873 Marsh built this magnificent home using carefully seasoned sugar pine for the interior woodwork. His granddaughter Lucille and her late husband James B. Christie restored the house in 1955.

Plaque dedicated 1977 by Chap 10 E Clampus Vitus: Lola Montez 1819-1861 Countess of Landsfeld. In her home which occupied this site, Lola's social salons 1853-1855 attracted men of vision whose investments and technology founded Nevada County's gold quartz mining industry. She brought culture and refinement to this rude mining camp. A mistress of international intrigue and a feminist before her time she is one of history's most recognizable women and a founder of today's cosmetic industry.

properties.Address: 16898 Hwy 49, Nevada City

Commander, purchased and reassembled a surplus WW II Quonset hut from the Navy and opened Bill Davis's Hut, a popular watering hole for the lumber and mining workforce. In 1950, Wilma Kenny leased the property and renamed it Wilma's Hut. Since then, the business was operated by a variety of individuals. In 1963, Bob and Peggy Tucker purchased the hut and renamed it Tuck's Hut. Then in 1969 the Tuckers leased the property to Frank Williams, owner of the Willo bar in Grass Valley, who was displaced by the Gold Country Freeway construction. He partnered with Veda Folden who, with the help of her husband and brothers, converted the covered structure into the main dining room. The Willo steakhouse was born. Many folks through the decades have asked why the Willo has no 'w' on the end (Willow). The Willo is a combination of Frank Williams last name and his wife's first name Lola. In 1976 Ken and Jeannie Hiebert purchased the property from Peggy Tucker and combined the bar and restaurant operations. They operated it for 26 years before selling it to the current owners, Mike Byrne and Nancy Wilson who at the time of this dedication are committed to preserving the California roadhouse heritage of the Willo, which has served over 1,000,000 choice New York steaks."

properties.Address: Along Hwy 174 between the Bear River and Brunswick Rd
properties.Desc_:
The Chicago Park Historic Agricultural Community occupies roughly the area on either side of Highway 174 between the Bear River and Brunswick Road. It is centered on the villages of Chicago Park and Peardale. In 1887, a group of Colfax and Chicago, Illinois developers acquired several thousand acres of land and drew up plans for the Chicago Park Colony. The Colony was to consist of 20 and 40 acre tracts as well as town lots laid out around a public square with streets named for prominent streets in Chicago. Much of the planned development never materialized, but reportedly almost 7000 acres were sold, principally to residents of Chicago. Many of the tracts were planted with orchards, and the area was referred to as the Bartlett Pear Belt. This historic community contains several landmarks and plaques.

properties.Address: Railroad Ave at back entrance to Northern Queen Inn, Nevada City

Plaque dedicated 2010 by Native Sons of the Golden West: The first hydraulic mining originated here at American Hill Diggins by Edward Matteson in 1853. Matteson originally used canvas hose. The canvas hose was replaced with crinoline hose in 1860. These miners' giants, also known as water cannons, monitors and dictators, washed hillsides away with high pressure water, uncovering gold bearing beds. This mining technique flourished profitably until 1884. Rivers were being filled with mud and debris causing flooding of the rich farm lands in the valley. At that time, a lawsuit brought by farmers against hydraulic mining was heard in Marysville, California where a decision known as The Sawyer Decision stopped all mining. Under a special use permit, granted by the Department of Fish and Game, these hydraulic monitors were last used at the Pacific Slab Mine near Foresthill, California in 1970, which was documented by the California Department of Parks and Recreation.

He named it the Dr. W. C. Jones Memorial Hospital for his father, who been the most prominent physician and surgeon in the county in the 19th century.  After John's death in 1917, his younger brother, Dr. Carl, continued the practice. The hospital opened in 1907 and served patients until 1968, being the area's principal medical center for most of that time. In 1975, it was acquired by Howard Levine and his wife the late Peggy Swan. Renamed the Swan Levine House, it is used as an arts academy and bed and breakfast inn.

Plaque dedicated 2018: Stevens Court honors John Christopher Stevens, United States Ambassador to Libya, who died in the service of his country September 11, 2012, in Benghazi. 'Chris' Stevens was born in Nevada County, the offspring of three generations of Grass Valleyans. Chris loved Grass Valley and spent many happy hours there. His fascination in foreign affairs and history led him to a Peace Corps stint in Morocco, followed by work in international legal law practice in San Francisco and Washington D.C. He then joined the Foreign Service, in which he served in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Jerusalem and Syria. When revolution broke out in Libya, Chris was sent out on a rusty Greek freighter to report and make recommendations for U.S. policy. His work led to appointment as U.S. Ambassador to the fledgling nation. Early on he established rapport with the Libyans, as he had with the people of the Middle East and Africa wherever he was stationed with the Foreign Service. Rather than hiding behind fortified walls, he strolled the streets, talking to the people. One day after the attack that cost him his life, thousands of Libyans took to the streets protesting his death. properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1993 by Nevada County, NEV 93-01. Photo display dedicated 1993 by Landmarks Commission: Early In the 1850's Glenbrook Basin first became known as the site of county fairs, horse racing and other special events. When Olympia Park, located at the south end of the basin, opened in 1901, Glenbrook Basin became the recreational center of Nevada County and much of Northern California, and remained so for over fifty years. People would come to the basin by horse and buggy or later the automobile, but those wishing for a little more excitement would often use the Nevada County Traction Company's trolley, or the Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad. The large grandstands of the three-quarter-mile racetrack stood near the junction of present Brunswick Road and Sutton Way. Trotting, pacing, and running horse races were held at the track, and motor car races began in 1913. The racetrack was one of the first electrically lighted racetracks in the state. A dam was constructed just northeast of the existing electrical substation to form Lake Olympia. The lake soon became one of the Basin's main attractions. Located in the center of Lake Olympia was an island with a pavilion which had a coil-spring-mounted dance floor that swayed with the rhythm of the dancers' feet. There was swimming, boating and fishing in Lake Olympia, and during some winters there was ice skating. There were boats and bathing suits for rent, and the park contained a bathhouse, a roller skating rink, and a bar. Many a romance blossomed on the lake during an evening boat ride under the stars. Families rented cabins and picnicked in the shade of the large pine trees along the shores of Lake Olympia. Olympia Park was the site of high school commencements, football and baseball games, and special events such as fat ladies' races and freckled-face children contests. The annual miners' picnics were held at the park with mucking and drilling contests, tug-of-wars and Cornish wrestling, as refreshments of various kinds flowed freely. Olympia Park fell into disrepair in the 1950s and ceased operation in 1958. Glenbrook Basin, once the recreational center for Nevada County, has developed into one of the county's main centers of commerce in supplying various types of shopping, restaurants, services and recreation for the residents and visitors of Nevada County.

Plaque dedicated 1994 by Native Sons of the Golden West: For 66 years, the Nevada City depot served as the northern terminus for the railroad affectionately known as the 'Never Come Never Go.' In 1874 a group of 7 men, led by lumber mill and gold mine owner John C. Coleman, organized the Nevada County Narrow Gauge Railroad. Engineer John Flint Kidder was hired on January 14, 1875 to build a 23 mile narrow gauge railroad from the Central Pacific Railroad connection in Colfax to Grass Valley and Nevada City. On a snowy May 20, 1876, John Coleman drove the last spike in Nevada City to dedicate the completion of the railroad. John Kidder controlled the railroad from January 1884, until his death on April 10, 1901; the following day, his widow Sara was elected president of the railroad. Sara Kidder successfully managed the company until its sale on April 24, 1913 to the Oakland, Antioch and Eastern, a predecessor to the Western Pacific. On May 13, 1926, the N.C.N.G.R.R. was purchased by a group of local investors and it operated until December 1942. The scrapping of the railroad was completed by May 5, 1943.

Landmark registered 2022 by Nevada County, NEV 22-03. Plaque dedicated 2022 by the Landmarks Commission in cooperation with the Celio Family: "In the 1850s, over 100,000 grapevines were planted in Nevada County, often by French settlers on the western part of the San Juan Ridge. For some years, Augustine Isoard operated a wine and liquor store in this building. On June 1, 1860, he advertised in the Nevada Journal that "I have on hand a few gallons of Wine manufactured from the Grape by myself, in this city." This is believed to be the first commercial winery operation in Nevada County. After a lull in the middle of the 20th century, commercial grape growing and winemaking came roaring back. Nevada County became part of the Sierra Foothills American Viticultural Area in 1987 and home to many wineries and hundreds of acres of grapes."

properties.Name: North Star Mine Powerhouse and Nevada County Traction Company
properties.Address: Allison Ranch Rd at McCourtney Rd, Grass Valley
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 1971 by State of California, CHL 843. First plaque dedicated 1971 by State in cooperation with Historical Society: The North Star Powerhouse, built by A. D. Foote in 1895, was the first complete water powered compressed air transmission plant of its kind. Compressed air, generated by Pelton water wheels, furnished power for the entire mine operation. The 30 foot Pelton wheel was the largest in the world, and was in continuous use for over 30 years.

Second plaque dedicated 1991 by American Society of Mechanical Engineers: International Mechanical Engineering Heritage Collection Pelton Water Wheel Collection North Star Power House Museum. The Pelton Wheel uses the momentum of a water jet impinging on buckets attached to the periphery of a wheel to produce power. It is a development of the primitive, so-called 'Hurdy Gurdy' wheel used in the California goldfields in the nineteenth century. Various inventors have contributed this type of water turbine, including Lester A. Pelton (1831-1908), who in 1880 patented the characteristic split bucket form. Subsequent important contributions to Pelton-Wheel technology were made by W. A. Doble. This collection illustrates the origin and development of the Pelton Waterwheel. American Society of Mechanical Engineers-1991.

Third plaque dedicated 1997 by Historical Society near smaller wheel: Pelton Type Water Wheel. Produced 71000 hp at 327 rpm, diameter 10 ft. Weight 26,000 lbs. Built by Allis Chalmers of single cast nickel steel. Gift of Oroville-Wyandotte Irrigation Dist.

properties.Name: Grass Valley AME Church and School Site
properties.Address: 315-323 S. Church Street, Grass Valley. Plaque located across the street in front of 328 S. Church.
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 2021 by Nevada County, NEV 21-02. Plaque dedicated 2022 by City of Grass Valley Historical Commission. "Across the street, on lots 315, 317, 319 and 323 S. Church Street, the Grass Valley African Methodist Episcopal Church and School were erected in 1854 and 1865 respectively by the local African American community. Reverend Peter Green and Church trustee and former slave Isaac Sanks, along with the other members of the congregation, worked to abolish slavery, secure voting rights for African American men, eliminate the ban on testimony of African Americans in court, and gain access to public accommodations and education. The AME Church was known for its exceptional choir and accomplished musicians. It was the site for fundraising events, literary readings, and the celebration of the Emancipation Proclamation. African American parents, whose children were denied entry into white schools, built their own schoolhouse next to the Church. Both the Church and School were sold in 1893 at public auction to Charles Clinch and the funds returned to the AME Church. Shortly thereafter, the new owners built the four Victorian homes that still stand on the property today."

properties.Name: Ellen Sargent
properties.Address: Calanan Park
properties.Desc_:
Landmark registered 2020 by Nevada County, NEV 20-03. Plaque dedicated 2020 by The Grand Parlor of the Native Daughters of the Golden West, The Captain John Oldham Chapter, NSDAR and the NC Historical Society. "Ellen Clark Sargent, a native of Massachusetts, arrived in Nevada City in 1852.  A leader in the fight for women's right to vote, she founded the Nevada County Woman's Suffrage Association in 1869. She was the President of the California Woman Suffrage Association and Treasurer of the National Woman Suffrage Association. Her tireless work resulted in California women winning the right to vote in 1911. Her campaign for national women's suffrage led to the introduction in 1878 of the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution by her husband, U.S. Senator A. A. Sargent. After many hard-fought battles by the Women's Suffrage Movement, the 19th Amendment was finally enacted into law on August 26, 1920."

See Sargent Homestead landmark.

Located: Calanan Park, Nevada City CA
